newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China-backed red chips to soar on Hong Kong market.
newsitem.headline: China-backed red chips to soar on Hong Kong market.

text.p: Red-chip fever, which raged on the Hong Kong market and dominated trading last week, is set to continue despite the high valuations of some of the China-backed, Hong Kong-incorporated companies, analysts said.

Eight of the market's 10 most actively traded shares on Friday were red-chips, with international banking giant HSBC Holdings Plc and Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd the only blue chips managing to retain a ranking.
"The red chips are strong, very strong," said Michael Ng, dealing director at Sassoon Securities.
Asset injections by mainland-based parent companies at low prices is the fuel driving the red-chip rave, analysts said.

Leading the red-chip sector last week was China Merchants Hai Hong Holdings Ltd The share price climbed more than 41 percent over the week, mainly due to stock exchange approval of its plans to acquire assets from its parent company and the success of its HK$3.87 billion fund-raising exercise.
The share closed HK$0.70 higher at HK$8.55 on Friday.
Chartists said most of the red chips were overbought and due for a correction.
"Turnover on red chips is at a record high, indicating there is a lot of selling already." said Charles Cheung, executive director at J&A Securities.
Still, some brokers love the red chips' growth stories and are not concerned about the high valuations.
"Traditional share valuations and techniques such as P/Es and discounts to NAVs (net asset values) don't work with these stocks,"said Chris Geiger, associate director at Vickers Ballas.

"Yesterday, China Merchants Hai Hong bought assets equal to 88 percent of its existing assets. The company has virtually doubled in size," said Geiger. "If these companies can do that, why shouldn't investors buy them."
Others see these share prices as unsustainable and lacking solid fundamentals.
"We have gotten to the silly stage," said Janet Gillies, sales director at OCBC Securities. "People are buying anything at any price, investing blindfolded."
Gillies said she had been recommending selected red chips for the past year, but was now calling for profit-taking.
"I am quite bearish as the whole market looks dangerous," said Lawrence Ang, head of China research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
But despite the warning signs, red chips were likely to continue to be the focus of the market for the coming four weeks or more, he added.
"The red chip euphoria is not over yet," agreed analyst Alex Tang of Yamaichi International (HK), who follows red chips.
Yamaichi International's red-chip index has risen more than 15 percent so far this month, compared with a 0.9 percent increase on the Hang Seng Index in the same period.
Demand for red chip shares was further fueled on Friday by the issue of call warrants on baskets of red chips by Merrill Lynch International, Peregrine Derivatives and BZW Warrants.
"It is possible that (red-chip) prices are going to peak, but the questions is when," said Sassoon's Ng.
Brokers said red chips were being bought by investors across the board, including mainland Chinese, local individuals and overseas-based institutions.
Yamaichi's Tang said part of the buying interest was related to the territory's impending handover to Chinese rule on July 1.

"Red chip prices are unlikely to peak until July 1," said Tang. "Beijing has said horse racing and dancing will continue in Hong Kong (after the handover) and (I bet) stock speculation will continue too," he added.
